name: Chapter 10: Cell Cycle and Cell Division
description: Cell cycle phases, G0, mitosis stages, cytokinesis, meiosis I and II, and their significance

cards.term: What is the cell cycle?
cards.definition: The sequence of events by which a cell duplicates its genome, synthesises other constituents and divides into two daughter cells

cards.term: Which three processes must be coordinated in a cell cycle?
cards.definition: Cell division, DNA replication and cell growth

cards.term: Is cell growth continuous? Is DNA synthesis?
cards.definition: Cytoplasmic growth is continuous; DNA synthesis happens only in one stage (S phase)

cards.term: How long is the cell cycle of human cells in culture?
cards.definition: About 24 hours

cards.term: How long is the yeast cell cycle?
cards.definition: About 90 minutes

cards.term: Two basic phases of the cell cycle?
cards.definition: Interphase and M phase (mitosis phase)

cards.term: In a 24-hour human cell cycle, how long does M phase last?
cards.definition: About 1 hour

cards.term: What fraction of the cell cycle is interphase?
cards.definition: More than 95%

cards.text: M phase starts with {{c1::karyokinesis}} (nuclear division) and usually ends with {{c2::cytokinesis}} (division of cytoplasm).

cards.term: Why is calling interphase the "resting phase" misleading?
cards.definition: The cell is not resting: it grows and replicates DNA in preparation for division. Only the nucleus looks inactive under the microscope.

cards.term: Figure 10.1 · Cell cycle
cards.definition: The narrow black arc is M phase; the wide yellow arcs are interphase (G1, S, G2).

cards.term: What happens in G1 phase?
cards.definition: The cell is metabolically active and grows continuously, but does not replicate DNA

cards.term: G1 phase is the interval between which two events?
cards.definition: End of mitosis and initiation of DNA replication

cards.term: What happens in S phase?
cards.definition: DNA replication: DNA per cell doubles

cards.term: DNA content goes from __ to __ in S phase.
cards.definition: 2C → 4C

cards.term: Does chromosome number change in S phase?
cards.definition: No. A 2n cell stays 2n; each chromosome now has two chromatids.

cards.term: In animal cells, what duplicates in the cytoplasm during S phase?
cards.definition: The centriole

cards.term: What happens in G2 phase?
cards.definition: Proteins are synthesised in preparation for mitosis; cell growth continues

cards.term: Intuition: why does counting chromosomes not double in S phase?
cards.definition: Chromosomes are counted by centromeres. After S, each chromosome has two sister chromatids joined at one centromere, so the count stays the same.

cards.term: Onion root tip cell has 16 chromosomes. Number at G1, after S, after M?
cards.definition: 16, 16, 16

cards.term: If DNA after M phase is 2C, what is it at G1, after S and at G2?
cards.definition: 2C, 4C, 4C

cards.term: What is the quiescent stage (G0)?
cards.definition: An inactive stage that cells exit G1 into; they stay metabolically active but do not proliferate unless required

cards.term: Example of adult animal cells that do not appear to divide?
cards.definition: Heart cells

cards.term: Are G0 cells metabolically dead?
cards.definition: No. They are metabolically active; they just do not divide.

cards.term: In animals, which cells show mitosis?
cards.definition: Only diploid somatic cells (with exceptions)

cards.term: Example of haploid animal cells that divide by mitosis?
cards.definition: Male honey bees (drones develop from unfertilised eggs)

cards.term: Can plants show mitosis in haploid cells?
cards.definition: Yes: plants divide mitotically in both haploid and diploid cells, e.g. the haploid gametophyte of mosses and ferns

cards.term: Why is mitosis called equational division?
cards.definition: Chromosome number in parent and progeny cells is the same

cards.term: Four stages of karyokinesis?
cards.definition: Prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase

cards.term: Mnemonic for the mitosis stages in order?
cards.definition: "I P-MAT": Interphase, then Prophase, Metaphase, Anaphase, Telophase

cards.term: Are the stages of mitosis sharply separated?
cards.definition: No. Division is a progressive process; clear-cut lines cannot be drawn.

cards.term: What marks the start of prophase?
cards.definition: Initiation of condensation of chromosomal material

cards.term: What are prophase chromosomes made of?
cards.definition: Two chromatids attached at the centromere

cards.term: What does the centrosome do in prophase?
cards.definition: The duplicated centrosome moves towards opposite poles

cards.term: What are asters?
cards.definition: Microtubules radiating from each centrosome

cards.term: What is the mitotic apparatus?
cards.definition: The two asters together with the spindle fibres

cards.term: Which structures are not seen at the end of prophase?
cards.definition: Golgi complex, ER, nucleolus and the nuclear envelope

cards.term: Plant cells lack centrioles. How do they form a spindle?
cards.definition: Spindle fibres organise without centrioles or asters (an anastral spindle). NCERT describes the animal-cell pattern.

cards.term: Identify this stage of mitosis.
cards.definition: Early prophase: chromatin begins to condense; nuclear envelope still intact

cards.term: Identify this stage of mitosis.
cards.definition: Late prophase: condensed chromosomes; nuclear envelope breaking up

cards.term: What marks the start of metaphase?
cards.definition: Complete disintegration of the nuclear envelope

cards.term: At which stage is chromosome morphology best studied?
cards.definition: Metaphase: condensation is complete

cards.term: What are kinetochores?
cards.definition: Small disc-shaped structures on the surface of centromeres, where spindle fibres attach

cards.term: What is the metaphase plate?
cards.definition: The plane of alignment of chromosomes at the equator in metaphase

cards.term: In metaphase, how are sister chromatids attached to the spindle?
cards.definition: Each chromatid, by its kinetochore, to fibres from opposite poles

cards.term: Key features of metaphase?
cards.definition: Spindle fibres attach to kinetochores; chromosomes align on the metaphase plate

cards.term: Identify this stage.
cards.definition: Transition to metaphase: chromosomes being moved to the equator by spindle fibres

cards.term: Identify this stage of mitosis.
cards.definition: Metaphase: all chromosomes lined up at the equator

cards.term: Why is metaphase used to make karyotypes?
cards.definition: Chromosomes are most condensed and spread out, so their number, size and centromere position are easiest to see. (Colchicine arrests cells at metaphase for this.)

cards.term: What happens at the onset of anaphase?
cards.definition: Each chromosome splits; sister chromatids (now daughter chromosomes) move to opposite poles

cards.term: In anaphase, which part of the chromosome leads towards the pole?
cards.definition: The centromere; the arms trail behind

cards.term: Key events of anaphase?
cards.definition: Centromeres split, chromatids separate and move to opposite poles

cards.term: Identify this stage of mitosis.
cards.definition: Anaphase: daughter chromosomes pulled to the poles, centromeres leading (V shapes)

cards.term: What happens to chromosomes in telophase?
cards.definition: They reach the poles, decondense and lose their individuality

cards.term: Key events of telophase?
cards.definition: Chromosomes cluster at poles; nuclear envelope re-forms around each cluster; nucleolus, Golgi, ER re-form

cards.term: Telophase is the reverse of which stage?
cards.definition: Prophase: chromosomes decondense and the nuclear envelope and nucleolus return

cards.term: Identify this stage of mitosis.
cards.definition: Telophase: two daughter nuclei forming; furrow starting

cards.term: What is cytokinesis?
cards.definition: Division of the cytoplasm into two daughter cells

cards.term: How does cytokinesis happen in animal cells?
cards.definition: A furrow in the plasma membrane deepens and joins in the centre

cards.term: How does cytokinesis happen in plant cells?
cards.definition: A cell plate forms in the centre and grows outward to meet the lateral walls

cards.term: Why can't plant cells use a furrow?
cards.definition: They are enclosed by a relatively inextensible cell wall

cards.term: What does the cell plate represent?
cards.definition: The middle lamella between the walls of two adjacent cells

cards.text: Animal cytokinesis goes from the {{c1::outside inwards (furrow)}}; plant cytokinesis goes from the {{c2::centre outwards (cell plate)}}.

cards.term: What is a syncytium? Example?
cards.definition: A multinucleate condition when karyokinesis is not followed by cytokinesis, e.g. liquid endosperm of coconut

cards.term: Which stage does this panel show?
cards.definition: Cytokinesis complete: two daughter cells. (NCERT labels this panel "Interphase (e)", meaning the daughter cells have entered interphase.)

cards.term: Mitosis is usually restricted to which cells?
cards.definition: Diploid cells. Exception: haploid cells of some lower plants and social insects.

cards.term: What do daughter cells of mitosis have?
cards.definition: An identical genetic complement (diploid)

cards.term: List the significance of mitosis.
cards.definition: Growth of multicellular organisms; restoring the nucleo-cytoplasmic ratio; cell repair; continuous growth of plants via meristems

cards.term: Why must a growing cell divide? (nucleo-cytoplasmic ratio)
cards.definition: Cytoplasm grows faster than the nucleus's control capacity; division restores the ratio

cards.term: Which cells are constantly replaced by mitosis?
cards.definition: Upper epidermis, gut lining, blood cells

cards.term: Which plant tissues give continuous growth by mitosis?
cards.definition: Meristems: apical and lateral cambium

cards.term: What is meiosis?
cards.definition: A division that halves the chromosome number, producing haploid daughter cells

cards.term: Where does meiosis occur?
cards.definition: During gametogenesis in plants and animals

cards.term: Meiosis ensures the haploid phase; what restores the diploid phase?
cards.definition: Fertilisation

cards.term: How many nuclear divisions and DNA replications in meiosis?
cards.definition: Two divisions (meiosis I and II), but only one DNA replication

cards.term: Key features of meiosis?
cards.definition: Pairing of homologous chromosomes, recombination between non-sister chromatids, and four haploid cells at the end

cards.term: Between which chromatids does recombination occur?
cards.definition: Non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes

cards.term: Mnemonic for the prophase I substages?
cards.definition: "Lazy Zebras Prefer Drinking Daily": Leptotene, Zygotene, Pachytene, Diplotene, Diakinesis

cards.term: Prophase I vs prophase of mitosis?
cards.definition: Prophase I is longer and more complex

cards.term: What happens in leptotene?
cards.definition: Chromosomes become gradually visible; compaction continues

cards.term: What happens in zygotene?
cards.definition: Homologous chromosomes start pairing: synapsis

cards.term: What is synapsis?
cards.definition: Pairing of homologous chromosomes (in zygotene)

cards.term: What accompanies synapsis (seen in electron micrographs)?
cards.definition: The synaptonemal complex

cards.term: What is a bivalent?
cards.definition: The complex of a pair of synapsed homologous chromosomes; also called a tetrad

cards.term: Why is a bivalent also called a tetrad?
cards.definition: It contains two chromosomes = four chromatids

cards.term: Which of the first three substages is the longest?
cards.definition: Pachytene (leptotene and zygotene are short-lived)

cards.term: What happens in pachytene?
cards.definition: Four chromatids of each bivalent become distinct (tetrads); crossing over between non-sister chromatids

cards.term: What are recombination nodules?
cards.definition: Sites where crossing over occurs (appear in pachytene)

cards.term: What is crossing over?
cards.definition: Exchange of genetic material between homologous chromosomes

cards.term: Which enzyme mediates crossing over?
cards.definition: Recombinase

cards.term: What marks the beginning of diplotene?
cards.definition: Dissolution of the synaptonemal complex; homologues begin to separate except at crossover sites

cards.term: What are chiasmata?
cards.definition: The X-shaped structures where homologues stay joined at crossover sites (diplotene)

cards.term: In which cells can diplotene last months or years?
cards.definition: Oocytes of some vertebrates

cards.term: Intuition: human oocytes and diplotene?
cards.definition: Human primary oocytes start meiosis before birth and pause in diplotene (dictyotene) until ovulation, which can be 12–50 years later

cards.term: What marks diakinesis?
cards.definition: Terminalisation of chiasmata

cards.term: What else happens in diakinesis?
cards.definition: Chromosomes fully condensed; meiotic spindle assembles; by its end the nucleolus and nuclear envelope disappear

cards.term: Diakinesis is a transition to which stage?
cards.definition: Metaphase I

cards.term: Prophase I substages: key event
cards.definition: Chromosomes become visible: Leptotene; Synapsis, synaptonemal complex: Zygotene; Crossing over, recombination nodules: Pachytene; Chiasmata visible: Diplotene; Terminalisation of chiasmata: Diakinesis

cards.term: What happens in metaphase I?
cards.definition: Bivalents align on the equatorial plate; microtubules from opposite poles attach to kinetochores of homologous chromosomes

cards.term: What happens in anaphase I?
cards.definition: Homologous chromosomes separate; sister chromatids stay together at their centromeres

cards.term: What happens in telophase I?
cards.definition: Nuclear membrane and nucleolus reappear; cytokinesis follows, forming a dyad of cells

cards.term: Do chromosomes fully decondense after telophase I?
cards.definition: No. They may disperse somewhat but do not reach the extended interphase state.

cards.term: What is interkinesis?
cards.definition: The short stage between the two meiotic divisions

cards.term: Does DNA replicate in interkinesis?
cards.definition: No

cards.term: Figure 10.3 · Stages of meiosis I
When does meiosis II begin?
cards.definition: Immediately after cytokinesis, usually before chromosomes have fully elongated

cards.term: Meiosis II resembles which division?
cards.definition: A normal mitosis

cards.term: Prophase II vs prophase I?
cards.definition: Prophase II is much simpler

cards.term: What happens in metaphase II?
cards.definition: Chromosomes align at the equator; microtubules attach to kinetochores of sister chromatids

cards.term: What happens in anaphase II?
cards.definition: Centromeres split; sister chromatids move to opposite poles by shortening of microtubules

cards.term: What happens in telophase II?
cards.definition: Nuclear envelope re-forms; cytokinesis gives a tetrad of cells: four haploid daughter cells

cards.term: Figure 10.4 · Stages of meiosis II
Anaphase of mitosis vs anaphase I of meiosis?
cards.definition: Mitosis: sister chromatids separate (centromere splits). Anaphase I: homologous chromosomes separate; centromere does not split.

cards.term: Which is the reduction division: meiosis I or II?
cards.definition: Meiosis I halves the chromosome number; meiosis II is equational

cards.term: A cell with 2n = 8 enters meiosis. Chromosomes per cell after meiosis I and after meiosis II?
cards.definition: 4 (each with 2 chromatids), then 4 (single chromatids)

cards.term: Mitosis vs meiosis
cards.definition: Divisions: Mitosis 1 · Meiosis 2; Daughter cells: 2 diploid · 4 haploid; Synapsis & crossing over: Absent · present (prophase I); Daughter cells identical?: Yes · no (variation); Where: Somatic cells · gamete-forming cells

cards.term: Can there be DNA replication without cell division?
cards.definition: Yes: endoreduplication, e.g. polytene chromosomes of Drosophila salivary glands

cards.term: Where are the four meiotic products unequal in size?
cards.definition: Oogenesis: one large ovum and small polar bodies. (Spermatogenesis gives four equal sperms.)

cards.term: Significance of meiosis?
cards.definition: Conserves the chromosome number of a species across generations; increases genetic variability

cards.term: What is paradoxical about meiosis conserving chromosome number?
cards.definition: It conserves the number across generations by halving it in gametes; fertilisation doubles it back

cards.term: Why is variation from meiosis important?
cards.definition: Variations are the raw material for evolution

cards.term: Two sources of variation in meiosis?
cards.definition: Crossing over (pachytene) and independent assortment of homologues (metaphase I / anaphase I)
